title: The man-eating king
hook: a prince keeps his word to return to a captor, and changes him (Jataka 537)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chaddanta, the wounded elephant who cut his own tusks for the man who shot him. Your line: he helped the hunter. Today, a prisoner who walks back to his captor.

It starts with a promise to a stranger. A traveling brahmin arrives with verses to teach, and Prince Sutasoma tells him: wait here, I'll hear them when I come back from my bath. He never makes it back. On the road, a man who eats people snatches him and carries him into the forest. Now the prince has a promise he can't keep, and a captor with no reason to let him go.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A STRANGER.` → `SNATCHED ON THE ROAD.` → `A PROMISE HE CAN'T KEEP.`

segments.voice: The captor, the Jataka says, was once a king who acquired a taste for human flesh, was driven from his kingdom, and now lives in the forest as a man-eater. Carried off, Sutasoma weeps, and the man-eater mocks him for fearing death. That's not why I'm crying, the prince says. I made a promise to a brahmin and left it unkept. Let me go, and I'll keep it, and I'll come back. The man-eater lets him go, sure he'll never see him again. Sutasoma goes home, hears the verses, rewards the brahmin. His family begs him to stay. He goes back anyway, alone, to the man who plans to eat him. The man-eater is stunned. Who walks back to his own death to keep a word? He asks to hear the verses, and they're about the worth of keeping company with good people. He offers the prince a gift for each one. Among the gifts Sutasoma asks for: give up eating human flesh, and set your captives free. The man-eater agrees, and the captives go home. Nothing here is forced. No army, no trick. The captor is changed by watching someone keep a promise that cost him everything. Tradition reads it as a picture of sacca, truthfulness, one of the ten perfections.
screen: `A KING TURNED MAN-EATER.` · `HE WEEPS FOR A PROMISE.` · `HE WALKS BACK ALONE.` · `HE ASKS: STOP.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you said you'd do that's still open: a call, a favor, a 'let me get back to you.' Picture actually doing it, where you'll be and what you'll say, and let any reluctance be there without fighting it while you hold the picture of the promise kept.
Sacca. Truth, truthfulness: the perfection behind the man-eating king who let Prince Sutasoma go, never expecting him back, and was changed when he returned. Today's word.
Your line: he came back. A kept word did what a sword couldn't. That's day eight hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Sutasoma story as an example of truthfulness (sacca), one of the ten perfections; keeping one's word is part of right speech in everyday practice.

original.note: Pali sacca: truth, and truthfulness, the perfection Sutasoma's kept word shows.

chat.says: What changed the man-eater in the Sutasoma story?
options: Watching the prince come back to keep his word, though it could cost his life.
The prince's soldiers surrounded the forest and forced him to stop.
The brahmin's verses scared him with threats of punishment after death.
chat.meaning: Nothing was forced. The man-eater was stunned that anyone would walk back to keep a promise, and asked to hear the verses.

Sutasoma.meaning: the prince who came back to keep his promise

brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class in old India

Jataka.meaning: the collection of tales of the Buddha's past lives

notes: Confirm: the brahmin (Nanda) arrives with verses; Sutasoma promises to hear them after bathing; the man-eater (Porisada) seizes him; he weeps over the unkept promise; he returns after rewarding the brahmin; the verses concern association with the good; he asks for one boon per verse and asks the man-eater to give up human flesh; the captive kings are freed.
